lesson.title: Molecular Handshakes: Why Specificity Is the Whole Point of Receptor Binding
lesson.summary: A receptor recognizes its signaling molecule, or ligand, through a precise three-dimensional fit shaped by the receptor's protein structure, and this specific, reversible binding event is what launches every signaling pathway.
lesson.body:
Every signaling pathway begins with an act of molecular recognition: a signaling molecule, called a ligand, must find and bind a receptor protein shaped to accept it. This is not a vague chemical attraction. A receptor's binding site is a three dimensional pocket built from the folded tertiary structure of the receptor protein, lined with specific amino acid side chains positioned to form hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, and hydrophobic contacts with one particular ligand or a small family of closely related ligands. Because binding depends on this precise geometric and chemical fit, a receptor built to bind epinephrine will not respond to insulin, even though both circulate in the same bloodstream at the same time.

Ligand binding is usually described with an induced fit model rather than a rigid lock and key model: the receptor's binding pocket is not a perfectly preformed mold but instead shifts slightly as the ligand settles in, and this shift is often what triggers the receptor's conformational change and downstream signaling activity. Binding is also reversible. Ligand and receptor associate and dissociate constantly, and the strength of that association, called binding affinity, determines how much ligand is needed before enough receptors are occupied to produce a response. High affinity receptors can respond to very low concentrations of hormone, while lower affinity interactions require much more ligand present before a response appears at all.

The receptors that carry out this recognition are themselves proteins, and their function is a direct consequence of principles covered earlier: a change anywhere in the amino acid sequence that alters the folded tertiary structure of the binding pocket can destroy a receptor's ability to recognize its ligand, which is exactly what happens in many inherited receptor diseases. Many receptors are also membrane proteins, integral proteins embedded in the plasma membrane with a portion exposed to the extracellular fluid, where it can encounter water soluble ligands that cannot cross the lipid bilayer on their own. The membrane anchors the receptor in place and orients it so its binding site faces outward while the part that changes shape and triggers a response faces the cytoplasm.

Binding is only useful because it does something: occupying the binding site pulls the receptor into a new shape, and that shape change is what gets read out by the rest of the signaling machinery, whether that means exposing a new surface for a G protein to dock onto, or bringing two receptor subunits together so their cytoplasmic tails can interact. Because binding is a probabilistic, reversible process governed by the concentrations of ligand and receptor, the fraction of receptors occupied, and therefore the strength of a cell's response, rises smoothly with ligand concentration up to a saturation point where essentially every receptor is occupied and adding more ligand no longer increases the response.

This binding event is the foundation on which every later stage of signaling is built. The next sections classify receptors by where they sit in the cell and how they convert binding into a transduced signal: receptors embedded in the plasma membrane that respond to ligands too large or too polar to cross it, and receptors located inside the cell that respond to small lipid soluble ligands able to slip through the membrane on their own. In both cases, the underlying principle established here, that specific, reversible, structurally determined binding is what launches the pathway, holds true.
